extracted.intended_audience: users and designers of TeX/Plain TeX systems (authors, typists, format designers, implementers)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and conventions for how TeX reads input characters, tokenizes them, maps character codes and accents, handles fonts/ligatures, and accepts dimension specifications and magnification. Covers control-sequence scanning, category codes, special notations (\char, ^^), accent conventions, and dimension syntax/limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uppercase/lowercase transformations use \uccode/\lccode
rubrics_metrics.description: The character is replaced by its \uccode value (unless zero), and conversion to lowercase uses \lccode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When INITEX begins most \uccode and \lccode values are zero except letters a–z and A–Z; \uppercase and \lowercase are performed during final scanning ('in its stomach') while some operations (\string, \number, \romannumeral, \csname) are carried out earlier (en route to the stomach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Access any font character with \charhnumberi
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \charhnumberi where hnumberi is 0–255 to obtain the corresponding character from the current font.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Append an optional space after the number. Example: \char37 is a percent sign; plain format defines \% as abbreviation for \char‘\% (i.e., \chardef\%=‘\%). Use when a needed symbol isn't available as a control sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal character codes based on ASCII
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX uses ASCII internal character codes (0–255) regardless of external file encoding; letters like 'b' are 98 internally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TeX converts external files to its internal code and back on output so results are machine-independent; Appendix C gives full details. Implementations should map external encodings to TeX's internal ASCII codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative numeric notations for character codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Character numbers may be given in octal (leading '), hexadecimal (leading "), or as plain decimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \char'142, \char"62, \char98 are equivalent. Valid octal range '0 to '377; hexadecimal range "0 to "FF. The manual sometimes uses typographic conventions for octal vs hexadecimal digits.

rubrics_metrics.name: ^^ notation for character codes
rubrics_metrics.description: The token ‘' when followed by a character or single-character control sequence stands for TeX's internal code for that character; ^^ sequences also permit ^^^^hex forms (^^00–^^ff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \char‘b equals \char98; ^^? is code 127; ^^M denotes ASCII return (13) and is significant; ^^I denotes tab. The ^^ convention is sometimes used in TeX's output.

rubrics_metrics.name: \chardef for associating names to character codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \chardef\<control sequence>=<hnumberi> to efficiently associate a control sequence name with a character code (0–255).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format designers often use \chardef to define special symbols (e.g., \chardef\%=‘\%). It's more efficient than \def for this purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: \char cannot appear in the middle of a control sequence name
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot use \char inside a control sequence name; e.g., \\char98 is parsed as \\ then letters c,h,a,r, etc., not as a single control sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits some dynamic naming techniques; use other constructs (e.g., \csname) when building names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category codes (\catcode) determine tokenization and are fixed when tokenized
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character has one of sixteen category codes which determine TeX's action; once characters become tokens their category is fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing \catcode is powerful but delicate: arguments to macros are tokenized with current categories, so changing categories after tokenization does not affect already-created token lists. The author discourages frequent \catcode changes except in unusual circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: States N, M, S determine input scanning behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX's reader is in one of three states: N (beginning of line), M (middle of line), or S (skipping blanks); these states affect how characters are handled (especially spaces and end-of-line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At beginning of every line TeX is in N; most of the time M; after control word or a space it is in S. Many rules about converting characters to tokens depend on current state.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-line handling depends on state
rubrics_metrics.description: When TeX sees an end-of-line character (category 5): in state N it becomes control sequence token 'par' (end of paragraph); in M it becomes a space token (code 32, category 10); in S it is dropped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TeX first deletes trailing spaces on a line then inserts an endlinechar (\endlinechar, normally 13) unless the line arose during error recovery. You can change \endlinechar; if negative or >255 nothing is appended (acts like a comment char).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spaces are handled by state-dependent rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A character of category 10 (space) is ignored in states N or S; in state M it becomes a space token (code 32) and TeX enters state S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spaces after control words are never turned into space tokens because state transitions ensure they are skipped; this explains why spaces after control words are ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment and ignored characters behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Category 14 (comment) causes TeX to throw away that character and the rest of the line; category 9 (ignored) is bypassed as if not present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use % (as defined in plain TeX) for comments. Ignored characters produce no effect and leave the state unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalid character handling (category 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If TeX sees an invalid character it bypasses it, issues an error message, and remains in the same state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some high-numbered codes may be invalid until their catcode is changed (e.g., character 127 often has category 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control-sequence name scanning rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon seeing an escape (category 0): (a) if end of line, name is empty (like \csname\endcsname); (b) if next char is non-letter, name is that single symbol; (c) otherwise name is the sequence of letters up to the first nonletter or line end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After case (c) TeX goes into state S; after case (b) TeX goes into state M except when the non-letter is a space (category 10) in which case it goes into S. The whole name becomes a single control sequence token.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special superscript (^^) sequences produce character codes
rubrics_metrics.description: If TeX sees two superscript characters (category 7) followed by a character with code c<128, the two carets are deleted and 64 is added/subtracted to/from c; if followed by two lowercase hex digits 0–9 or a–f, the quartet is replaced by the single character with that hex code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacement is done even during control-sequence-name scanning. If a superscript is not the first of such a trio/quartet it is handled by the general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: General tokenization rule for most characters
rubrics_metrics.description: If TeX sees a character of categories 1,2,3,4,6,8,11,12,13, or a category-7 not part of a special sequence, it converts the character to a token attaching the category code and goes into state M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the normal case: almost every nonblank character is handled this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: ^ notation with two hex digits gives uniform 256-character access
rubrics_metrics.description: ^^ followed by two lowercase hexadecimal digits (0–9 or a–f) denotes characters from ^^00 to ^^ff uniformly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character 127 is ^^7f. Most ^^ codes are unimportant except in unusual applications; ^^M (^^13) and ^^I (tab) are noteworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on keyboard layout; format designers can remap characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Local formats can define \catcode and control sequences so that nonstandard keyboards (e.g., Norwegian æ at code 241) work, and may provide replacements (e.g., ^^f1) to make files portable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also arrange fonts so that the internal code prints as the desired glyph, and adapt hyphenation rules. For portability provide the format used to friends/machines without the keyboard symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligature and punctuation conventions in roman fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX's roman font treats sequences such as ff, fi, fl, ffi, ffl as ligatures; ‘‘ and ’’ as opening/closing double quotes; -- as en-dash, --- as em-dash; ?‘ and !‘ for inverted punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use math mode for + and = in formulas to get proper spacing; hyphen and slash usage differs between text and math modes. Ligature behavior is font dependent (\tt disables these ligatures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved characters in plain TeX and how to type them
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX reserves $ # % & ^ \ ~ { } _; to typeset the visible symbols type respectively \$ \# \% \& etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Braces and backslashes are available via control sequences in math mode; some symbols (", |, <, >) are not wanted in text and are handled differently or only in typewriter font.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accents and special letters via control sequences and \accent primitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides accent control sequences (\`o, \'o, \^o, \"o, \~o, \=o, \.o, \\u o, \\v o, \H o, \t oo) and under-accents (\c o, \d o, \b o); these are implemented using \accent< number> applied to the next character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accents are positioned for a character of x-height; TeX raises/lowers accents for taller/shorter characters and accounts for slantedness. The width of the constructed accented character equals the width of the base character. Mode-independent commands may appear between accent number and character but grouping must not intervene. If no suitable character is present the accent appears alone (e.g., \'{} produces ´). Use \i and \j for dotless i/j before accents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why accent macros use braces around argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX defines \'#1 as '{\accent19 #1}', not simply an abbreviation for \accent19, to ensure proper grouping and argument handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The braces protect the accent/argument grouping so the accent applies to exactly the intended token(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Font-specific conventions may differ; plain TeX conventions are not universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Accent and special-letter conventions described belong to the plain TeX format and Computer Modern fonts; different fonts/formats should provide their own rules and may, for instance, treat accents as ligatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For large-scale multilingual typesetting, designers should prefer font-specific treatments (e.g., ligatures for accented letters) rather than the plain TeX backslash conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typewriter font (\tt) differs: no ligatures and fixed-width characters
rubrics_metrics.description: In \tt ff, fi, etc., are not treated as ligatures; dashes and double-quotes are ordinary characters; some accent commands and certain letters (\H, \. , \l, \L) are unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In \tt you can type ", |, <, >; all characters in \tt have the same width, suitable for monospaced output or code imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain symbols are shared across families via math symbol font
rubrics_metrics.description: \dag, \ddag, \S, \P produce dagger, double dagger, section sign, paragraph sign and come from the math symbols font, appearing identically in \rm, \sl, \bf, \it, \tt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Appendix B for more non-math symbols; these specific symbols are available in all styles because they are taken from a math symbol font.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension syntax: form and allowed units
rubrics_metrics.description: A dimension is specified as optional-sign number unit (e.g., 3in or -.013837in) or optional-sign digitstring . digitstring unit; units: pt, pc, in, bp, cm, mm, dd, cc, sp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decimal point may be '.' or ','. Spaces optional before sign/number/unit but not within digit strings or unit letters. Examples: 3 in, -.013837in, 0.mm, 29 pc, +42,1 dd, 123456789sp. When dimension is zero you must include a unit (0pt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact unit conversion ratios and internal unit sp
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: pt point (manual baseline 12pt), pc pica (1pc=12pt), in inch (1in=72.27pt), bp big point (72bp=1in), cm (2.54cm=1in), mm (10mm=1cm), dd didot (1157dd=1238pt), cc cicero (1cc=12dd), sp scaled point (65536 sp = 1pt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TeX represents dimensions internally as integer multiples of sp for machine-independent arithmetic. 'pt' is slightly larger than the classical point to make conversion efficient; differences are negligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum legal dimension limit
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX will not handle dimensions whose absolute value is 230 sp or more (i.e., maximum legal dimension slightly less than 16384pt, about 18.892 feet / 5.7583 meters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bound is due to internal integer representation; be mindful when setting very large skips or sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: \magnification usage and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: To magnify output use \magnification=<number> where the number is 1000 times the factor f (e.g., \magnification=1200 for 1.2x); this instruction must be given before the first page of output is completed and you cannot apply two different magnifications to the same document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical magnifications: 1200 for 1.2×, 2000 for 2×. Magnification scales heights and widths, affecting area quadratically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with control words vs control symbols and spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Spaces after control words are ignored (they never become space tokens), and control symbols (escape followed by a non-letter) form single-character control sequences; this difference affects state transitions and spacing behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To get a space after a control word you can insert an explicit space or use braces; understanding state rules clarifies why plain TeX ignores spaces in some contexts.
